texts.facts: :: JUDGMENT : : This is a private complaint filed by the complainant against the accused for the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 2. The factual matrix of the complainant's case are as under; The complainant and accused are known to each other from past several years. In the month of August 2021 accused approached the complainant seeking financial assistance of Rs.3,00,000/- to meet his urgent legal necessities. Considering the request of the accused, JUDGMENT -3- C.C.3149/2022 complainant paid an amount of Rs.2,74,000/- on 01.08.2021 and accused promised to repay the same within a period of one month. After completion of one month complainant demanded the accused to repay the same, for which accused had issued two cheques bearing No.170716 for Rs.24,000/- dated 09.09.2021 and another cheque bearing No.115536 for Rs.2,50,000/- dated 30.09.2021 drawn on Indian Bank, Cubbonpet Branch, Bengaluru in favour of complainant. On presentation of the said cheques for encashment through his banker, the same were dishonored for the reason of "Funds Insufficient" in the account of the accused and Banker had issued memo. The complainant has got issued legal notice through his counsel on 19.10.2021 calling upon the accused to repay the amount within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice. The said notice was duly served on the accused. Inspite of that accused has failed to pay the cheques amount. Hence, the complainant has filed this present complaint. 3. In order to prove the case of the complainant, complainant got examined himself as PW.1 and got marked JUDGMENT -4- C.C.3149/2022 Ex.P1 to Ex.P8. This court after taking cognizance of the offence issued summons to the accused. 4. In pursuance of the summons, the accused has appeared through his counsel and he has got enlarged on bail. The sum and substance of the accusation has been read over to the accused and he has denied the same and not pleaded guilty and submitted that he has defence to make. The complainant during the course of further evidence, he has got marked the nine documents as Ex.P.9 to Ex.P.17 and during the course of cross-examination of DW1 counsel for the complainant has got marked three documents as Ex.P.18 to Ex.P.20. After completion of evidence of the complainant side, statement under section 313 of Cr.P.C. was recorded and the incriminating evidence appearing against the accused is read over and explained to the accused and he has denied the same and examined himself as DW1. The complainant in order to prove his case himself examined as PW1 and got marked documents as Ex.P.1 to Ex.P.8. Ex.P.1 and Ex.P.3 cheques are belongs to the accused.
texts.arguments: This aspect has been stated in the case of Vinaya Devanna Nayak V/s. Ryot Sewa Sahakari Bank Ltd., reported in 2008 (2) SCC 305, this decision has been in the case of Bir Singh V/s. Mukesh Kumar reported in (2019) 4 SCC 197. Sri L Keshavachandra vs Sri A Thipparaju @ Appajappa Thipparaju on 27 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/177273754/ 3 The main ingredients of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are:- (i) Drawing up of a cheque by accused towards payment of an amount of money, for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or any other liability; (ii) Return of the cheque by the Bank as unpaid; (iii) The drawer of the cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money within 30 JUDGMENT -7- C.C.3149/2022 days of the receipt of the notice under the proviso (b) to Section 138. The Explanation appended to the Section provides that, the "debt or other liability" for the purpose of this Section means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. Apart from this, Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act lays down a presumption in favour of the holder of cheque in the following terms:- "It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that:- The holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Sec. 138, for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability". Also, Sec. 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act states; "Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made:- (a) That every Negotiable Instrument was made or drawn for consideration and that every such instrument, when it has been JUDGMENT -8- C.C.3149/2022 accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration." Perusal of records it discloses that, the complainant has followed the procedure and time lines fixed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act from the date of dishonour of cheque till presentation of private complaint. If the accused has rebutted the case of the complainant, then the onus is shifts on the complainant, then the complainant has to prove his case independently, same has been held by the Hon'ble Apex court in Rangappa V/s. Mohan AIR 2010 SCC 1898. 11. The accused has to rebut the case of the complainant with preponderance of probabilities, if the accused has rebut the case of the complainant on preponderance of probabilities, then the onus shifts on the complainant to prove his case, the same has been held in the case of Basalingappa V/s. Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418 the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has summarized the principles on Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. JUDGMENT - 10 - C.C.3149/2022 12. 14. The counsel for the accused argued that, the accused had obtained the some amount as a loan from one Mr.Harish and hand over the 10 cheques for the purpose of security after repayment of the loan amount to the Harish he has not returned the said cheques. Further argued that, Harish and this complainant are friends, Harish is attending this court every date of hearing. Hence, the question of advancing the loan during Covid-19 pandemic to the accused does not arises and he relied on the ruling JUDGMENT - 12 - C.C.3149/2022 reported in 2023 (2) AKR 645 in the case of Jagadish Reddy Vs. G.Chandranna and pray for acquittal of the accused. 15. The counsel for the complainant argued that, the accused was not disputed the Ex.P.1, Ex.P3, Ex.P.1(a) and Ex.P.3(a) and moreover accused himself admitted the Ex.P.18 to Ex.P.20 during the course of cross-examination. Hence, document admitted by the accused itself are sufficient to hold that accused was obtained the hand loan of Rs.2,74,000/- from the accused and issued the Ex.P.1 and Ex.P.3 cheques and relied the ruling reported in 1) (2021) 5 SCC 283, Kalamani Tex and another Vs. P.Balasubramanian, 2) 2015 AIR SCW 3040, T.Vasanthkumar Vs. Vijayakumari and 3) 2022 (1) AKR 393, S.Venugopala Vs. S.H.Siddalingaswamy. As per Section 20 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881, Where a one person signs and delivers to another a paper stamped in accordance with the law relating to negotiable instruments then in force in India, and either wholly blank or having written thereon an incomplete negotiable instrument, he thereby gives prima facie authority to the holder thereof to make or complete as the case may be upon it a negotiable instrument, for any amount specified therein and not exceeding the amount covered by the stamp. 24. For that, complainant counsel relied the Judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court reported in (2021) 5 SCC 283 (Kalamani Tex and another V/s. P. Balasubramanian. In the said Judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court held, at Para No.13 while discussing the provisions of section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act that: "the statue mandates that once the signature of an accused on the cheque is established, then these "reverse onus" clauses become operative. In such a situation, the obligation shifts upon the accused to discharge the presumption imposed upon him." In the said Judgment, the Hon'ble Apex Court at Para No.17 has held that, "even if the arguments raised by the appellants are taken at face value that only a JUDGMENT - 20 - C.C.3149/2022 blank cheque and signed blank stamp papers were given to the respondent, yet the statutory presumption cannot be obliterated, because, legally, even a blank cheque leaf, voluntarily signed and handed over by the accused, which is towards some payment, would attract presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act." Further, I relied the Judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court reported in (2022) 7 SCR. 72 between Oriental Bank of Commerce V/s. The presumption which arises on the signing of the cheque cannot be rebutted merely by the report of a hand-writing expert.
